title: Query Optimisation: Searching
lead: There are too many correct plans to try them all. Build and reuse smaller candidates, while remembering the output order that later steps may need.
goals: Enumerate and cost access paths for a single table
Explain why the number of join trees grows rapidly
Distinguish left-deep, bushy, and right-deep join trees
Understand the benefits and limits of cross-product pruning

sections.title: Start search with a complete single-table comparison
sections.html:
Suppose costing can estimate a candidate, but the query has many possible candidates. Which should the optimizer generate and remember? Begin with the smallest problem: retrieve rows from one table. These single-table plans become building blocks for later joins.

Use an original table with 20,000 tuples on 200 data pages. An eligible index has 20 leaf pages. A predicate covers 5% of entries. To isolate the subsequent reads, omit internal tree descent from all index calculations; in a complete comparison add it separately.

CandidateLeaf readsTable retrievalApproximate total
Sequential heap scan0all 200 pages200
Clustered index0.05×20=10.05×200=10 pages11
Unclustered index, one uncached fetch per row0.05×20=10.05×20,000=1,000 fetches1,001

The same 5% retains 1,000 rows in both index cases. Clustering changes their placement, not their count. The unclustered estimate counts repeated fetches; 1,000 reads are not 1,000 distinct pages in a 200-page table. Caching or grouping RIDs can lower that model's total. Nor does 5% selectivity alone prove that clustered rows occupy exactly ten pages: this is an explicit distribution approximation.

At 100% selectivity, the clustered approximation reads 20+200=220 pages and the heap still reads 200, before descent overhead. An index can be eligible yet lose the comparison. For a unique-key equality lookup, count internal traversal, a leaf, and any required data fetch instead of multiplying whole-file sizes by an arbitrarily tiny fraction.

For each base table, enumerate supported access paths, include residual tests and any necessary duplicate elimination, and record useful output order as well as cost. A one-table query may also require GROUP BY or aggregation; finding rows is not necessarily its entire plan. Keep units and final requirements consistent before retaining a winner.

What extra information distinguishes the 11 and 1,001 estimates?

Physical clustering and fetch/cache assumptions. Row count and predicate fraction alone are identical, so they cannot explain the difference.

Key takeaway

Even at the same selectivity, clustering can change the best plan. Count index-page reads and data fetches separately. Do not substitute tuple counts for page counts without stating the assumption that justifies it.

sections.title: Limit the search without pretending excluded plans are impossible
sections.html:
For three tables, even the order and grouping of joins vary. An ordered binary tree has two shapes for three leaves, and the labels have 3!=6 orders: 12 syntactic join trees. Four leaves have five shapes and 4!=24 label orders, yielding 120. This convention counts left/right orientation separately, before equivalent cases are collapsed. We have not yet multiplied by access paths and join algorithms.

System R reduces the candidates by considering left-deep trees: every right input is one base table, and the left input can be a previous join result. For example, ((R join S) join T) join U. A right-deep tree reverses those roles; a bushy tree such as (R join S) join (T join U) has two intermediate inputs. Keeping one left-deep shape for four labeled tables leaves 24 leaf orders, rather than all 120 shapes/orders.

A base-table inner input can expose an index for nested-loop probes. Streaming a left result into successive joins can avoid temporary results. But a sort in that tree can still block: left-deep describes structure, not a guarantee of complete pipelining. Restricting the shape also excludes potentially good bushy plans.

Now take R(a), S(a,b), T(b) with predicates R.a=S.a and S.b=T.b. The join graph is R—S—T. A policy excluding Cartesian products keeps connected pairs RS and ST, and drops RT because it has no direct predicate under this fixture. Extend the retained pairs with the remaining table.

Understand the price of pruning

Suppose R and T each have two rows. Their Cartesian product has only four pairs. A supplied abstract cost model gives the connected RS route 20 to form RS and 15 to add T: 35 total. It gives R×T cost 2, then 8 to add S using both original predicates and a suitable (a,b) path: 10 total. These are supplied exercise costs, not numbers derived from the row counts.

The no-Cartesian-product policy discards the 10-unit route before costing it. It often saves search and avoids huge intermediates, but it can miss a cheaper candidate. Every retained or excluded candidate must still preserve both predicates; pruning a plan is different from dropping a query condition.

sections.title: Remember subplans together with their useful output order
sections.html:
Recomputing the best way to join R and S for every larger plan wastes optimization time. Dynamic programming (DP) saves a result for each smaller subproblem and reuses it. In this left-deep search, a pass means the number of tables in a subplan, not a pass over data pages.

  1. Pass 1: enumerate access paths for R, S, T and retain relevant choices.
  2. Pass 2: extend single-table entries into RS and ST, testing both orientations and eligible algorithms. Under our no-product policy, RT is absent.
  3. Pass 3: extend retained two-table entries with the missing base table, then include final operations required by the query.

Can we retain just one cheapest plan per subset? Suppose unordered RS costs 100, ordered RS costs 125, and the final query needs ORDER BY customer_id. Sorting the unordered result costs 80. Complete costs are 100+80=180 versus 125+0=125. Discarding the 125-cost subplan would lose the cheaper complete plan.

An interesting order is an output order useful to a later join, grouping, duplicate removal, or final ordering. The saved state therefore includes both relation subset and physical property. Retain the cheapest overall candidate and the cheapest for each relevant order; do not retain every expensive plan with an identical property.

Extend a ledger rather than choose a cheap partial number

Return to R(a), S(a,b), T(b). These supplied costs already include each subplan's selected access and join work. Assume only the last route preserves final order a.

Saved subset/propertySubplanAdd missing tableJoin totalAdd final ORDER BY aComplete total
RS, unordered40458530115
RS, ordered b52207230102
ST, unordered35508530115
ST, ordered a601070070

For RS, spending 12 extra units now (52−40) saves 25 on the extension (45−20), yielding 72 instead of 85. For the whole query, the a-ordered ST route wins at 70. The 35-unit ST subplan was cheapest alone but did not have the best extension.

DP can reuse “best” substructure only after defining the properties future operators need. Its result is best relative to retained shapes, access choices, physical-property model, and estimated costs. It is not a guarantee of the fastest real execution among every imaginable plan. Add GROUP BY, aggregation, and sorting costs above the chosen join rather than ending the ledger early.

Key takeaway

Retain plans with useful orders as well as the cheapest current plan. An interesting order is an order that may let a later join, GROUP BY, or ORDER BY avoid sorting again.

sections.title: Exercise: let the final requirement change the winner
sections.html:
A saved RS plan costs 40 and outputs 10 pages. A saved ST plan costs 30 and outputs 100 pages. Adding T to RS costs another 20; adding R to ST costs another 80. These are supplied costs in the same abstract unit, not a formula derived solely from the output-page counts. Which complete join route wins?

Compare complete joins

RS then T costs 40+20=60. ST then R costs 30+80=110. The 30-cost subplan loses despite being cheaper by itself. Its larger output may contribute to expensive later work, but the supplied extension costs, not page counts alone, determine this exercise.

Now final ordering costs 50 above the first route and 0 above the second. Recalculate instead of reusing the old winner. Then ask what happens if the first route's final sort costs 70 instead.

Include the requested final order

With a 50-unit sort: first route 60+50=110, second 110+0=110, a tie. With a 70-unit sort: first 130, second 110, so the second route wins. A required physical property can reverse the comparison.

Before accepting an optimizer claim, identify its retained search space and statistics. A search limited to left-deep connected plans can only choose among those plans. Better estimates or a broader space may change the choice, but exploring more candidates also takes optimization time. The objective is a correct answer with a low-cost complete plan, not the largest possible enumeration.

quiz.question: Why retain a more expensive subplan that already produces sorted output?
options: Because sorted output is always better
Because it may avoid an expensive sort later
Because subplan cost does not matter
quiz.explanation: An interesting order can reduce the total plan cost by avoiding a later sort, even if that subplan costs more.
